lede.text: Sanganeri hand block printing stamps designs on cloth with wooden hand blocks, mainly in Sanganer town and nearby villages of Jaipur district, on a white base, as the GI application specifies, with delicate floral motifs.
The GI application states that its art and skill are limited to the Chhipa community, while Kharadi turners make the blocks from dried shisham, gurjan, mango and teak wood.

George Watt called Sanganer the very metropolis of India's calico-printing craft in art conceptions and technique, and Ritu Kumar named fast colours and well-proportioned lyrical motifs as its printers' main contributions.
The GI application calls tapai, the sun bleaching that whitens a ground over-dyed by alizarin, the most typical part of Sanganeri production.

sentences.text: Sanganer was founded in the early 16th century by the Kachhwaha prince Sangaji and became a printing centre in later centuries.

No record of a Sanganer printing unit is traced before the early 18th century, and reports of 1703 describe taxes levied on printed fabrics, as do records of 1727 that speak of dyeing rather than printing.

Sources differ on when printers came from Gujarat: Incredible India dates their migration to the late 16th and early 17th century, while D'source says Sawai Jai Singh invited them in the 18th century.
Cloth printing developed at Sanganer during the 18th century and reached its peak in the 19th century, encouraged by the patronage of the Jaipur royal family.

George Watt called Sanganer the very metropolis of India's calico-printing craft in art conceptions and technique, yet found the once large and prosperous town reduced to dilapidated hovels of a few poorly paid calico-printers.
Screen printing came to Sanganer around 1960, taken up by Khatri printers from Mirpur and Sind.
Printing in Jaipur and Sanganer, with its small and delicate patterns, almost came to a halt by the middle of the 20th century and was revived in the 1970s.
Sources differ on the tradition's age: at least two hundred and fifty years, more than 300 years, or almost 500 years.

The GI application lists the production steps in this order: scouring, harda treatment called peela karna, mordant printing called chapai, ageing called sukhai, washing called khulai and dyeing called rangai.
Then come tapai sun bleaching, dhabu datai resist printing, neel rangai indigo dyeing, yellow dyeing, fitkari rangai alum fixing and the final wash called dhulai.
The printed cloth is aged for at least three to four days so the mordant paste penetrates the fibres.
Dyeing is done in large copper vessels heated by wood fire, with the alizarin filled in small cloth bags.
For sun bleaching the cloth is laid flat on a river bed and sprinkled with a mild solution of cow dung and water.
Dabu acts as a mechanical resist used only for indigo patterns, and sawdust sprinkled over it gives additional layers of resist.
Yellow from turmeric and pomegranate rind is rubbed on with a loose-woven woollen cloth and fixed by a dip of only a few minutes in diluted alum.
Block carving follows its own sequence of ghisai, chakai, khudai, dabana and chilai before a hatha handle is added.
Harda contains tannic acid, which attracts the mordants applied with the wooden blocks.
The tannic acid of harda forms a black colour with syahi, the ferrous mordant.
In dyeing, alizarin reacts with two mordants on one print, giving red with alum and black with ferrous.
Opened out after each dip, the cloth meets atmospheric oxygen, which turns reduced indigo into oxidised indigo, and dipping is repeated until the desired dark shade.
Alkali from the cow dung and heat from the sun's rays together bleach the ground colour white again.
In Sanganer's dyeing and printing units at present, a 2013 study reports, indigo and rapid dyes are fixed by diazotization in dilute sulfuric or hydrochloric acid with sodium nitrite.
The units' wastewater measured pH 6.8 to 7.3, near neutral, because salt and caustic slurry offset the acids.
Sanganeri textiles are mostly printed on cotton cloth, sometimes on cotton and silk, and fineness favoured the cotton muslin called mulmul.
Syahi is a fermented solution of iron with jaggery and gum; begar, the alum mordant, develops a rich red with alizarin, and Jain and Hada write that the red was made with alum and geru, a red soil.
The red bath was made from madder, which contains alizarin and purpurin, with dhawai flowers boiled in to give the required reddish hue.
Dabu paste is mixed from kali mitti, lime, wheat flour and gum, and every family keeps its own recipe secret.
Kharadi turners make the printing blocks from dried wood of shisham, gurjan, mango, teak and ardu.
Sanganer craftsmen use chemical dyes in abundance and natural dyes only for specific orders.
The GI application specifies that designs on Sanganeri textiles are necessarily repetitive and that every piece carries buti, buta or jhar designs or a combination of them.
Sources differ on the ground colour: the GI application specifies white, Watt found grounds usually white, blue or yellow, and D'source calls a yellow, green or blue background typical.
A buti is a very small motif, up to 20 to a block, while a buta is a single motif complete in itself, normally no bigger than 3 by 5 inches.

Black and red syahi begar designs on white cloth served the local community for safa turbans and angochha shawls, while floral motifs on white or soft-toned grounds were patronised at the Jaipur court.
Dupattas and shawls for Hindu temples bore red designs on white or yellow cloth, and prints imitating bandhani were made for women.
Mughal influence extended the motifs to flowers such as iris, tulip and narcissus, which were not grown in the area.
Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay wrote that a special feature of these prints is the use of a variety of designs in one cloth, beautifully harmonised.
The GI's area of production is mainly Sanganer town, headquarters of Sanganer tehsil in Jaipur district, and nearby villages.
Sources place Sanganer 15 or 16 kilometres from Jaipur, and the Imperial Gazetteer put it 7 miles south of Jaipur city on the Aman-i-Shah river.

Block-printing washers settled in Sanganer centuries ago because of its flowing river, the Christian Science Monitor reports, and traditionally washing the cloth many times in abundant water and drying it in the open sun gave the printing its characteristic touch.
Sources name different rivers: the Saraswati, whose abundant water is credited with the radiance of Sanganeri fabrics, and the Dhoondh, whose riverbanks served the dyers and bleachers.
A 2013 study found the wastewater of Sanganer's dyeing and printing units high in sodium, chloride and sulfate, with remarkable concentrations of copper, chromium and iron.
Discharged untreated on land, it reaches the Amanishah Nallah through small watercourses, and eleven groundwater samples from Sanganer were polluted by percolating wastewater.
The Asian Age reported that the Amanishah nullah was once the perennial Dravyavati river, whose dams were washed away in the downpour of 1981.
In 2015 the Rajasthan High Court held to its order closing polluting textile units without no-objection certificates, whose effluents were polluting the Draviyawati river.
The Calico Printers Cooperative Society filed GI application 147 on 2 December 2008, and the registry issued certificate 119 dated 19 March 2010.
Other sources date the GI tag to 2009, and the registry's document list includes a certificate of registration dated 19 March 2009.
The registry's record lists 253 authorised-user entries, not all of them marked registered, and the registration is valid up to 1 December 2028.
The GI application reported 315 printing units and more than twenty exporting units in Sanganer.

Counts for 2003 differ: a High Court sub-committee report gave 473 units in 8 clusters with around 2 lakh artisans, while the Times of India counted about 150 block print units employing about 3,000 families.

Screen-printed imitations are sold as genuine Sanganeri block prints, according to the GI application, and artisans of Bagru and Sanganer surveyed by Kathju and Kashyap said digital prints are passed off too.
In a 2025 study only half of the Sanganer artisans surveyed knew of the GI, and 96.9% did not use it as a marketing tool.
